---
title: Accuracy tests on the Hyperboloid
---


```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| code-fold: true
#| output: false
using Pkg;
cd(@__DIR__)
Pkg.activate("."); # for reproducibility use the local accuracy environment.
```

In this small note we compare different implementations of several functions on the
[Hyperbolic](../manifolds/hyperbolic.md).
We compare the functions prior to
[PR #631](https://github.com/JuliaManifolds/Manifolds.jl/pull/631) to those introduced therein.
We compare the previous version (always called `_1`) and the new version `_2`, where we leave out the manifold to indicate, that these are the local functions here.
We compare this to the one given in `Manifolds.jl` at time of writing (which is the first one), on `BigFloat` on several scales of magnitudes.

```{julia}
#| output: false
using Manifolds, Random, NamedColors, Plots, LinearAlgebra
using Manifolds: minkowski_metric

paul_tol = load_paul_tol()
indigo = paul_tol["mutedindigo"]
teal = paul_tol["mutedteal"]
```

## Reference Data

We choose a “base point”, a direction and create tangent vectors and corresponding points in several magnitudes of distances
```{julia}
#| output: false
M = Hyperbolic(2)
p = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]
pb = BigFloat.(p)
X = [1 / sqrt(2), 1 / sqrt(2), 0.0]
Xb = BigFloat.(X)
lengths = [10.0^k for k in -16:4]
Xbs = [s * Xb for s in lengths]
Xbns = [norm(M, p, X) for X in Xbs]
qbs = [exp(M, pb, Y) for Y in Xbs]
Xs = [Float64.(X) for X in Xbs]
qs = [Float64.(q) for q in qbs]
Xns = [norm(M, p, Y) for Y in Xs]
```

## Distance

We define

```{julia}
#| output: false
distance_1(p, q) = acosh(max(-minkowski_metric(p, q), 1.0))
function distance_2(p, q)
    w = q - p
    m = sqrt(max(0.0, minkowski_metric(w, w)))
    return 2 * asinh(m / 2)
end
```

and compare

```{julia}
d_1 = [distance_1(p, q) for q in qs]
d_2 = [distance_2(p, q) for q in qs]
fig = plot(;
    legend = :topleft,
    xlabel = raw"lengths $s$ (log. scale)",
    ylabel = raw"Error to BigFloat (log. scale)",
    yaxis = :log,
    xaxis = :log,
    ylims = (1.0e-34, 1.0e2),
    xlims = (1.0e-17, 10^3),
)
plot!(fig, lengths, abs.(Xbns .- d_1), color = indigo, label = "1 - acosh-based")
plot!(fig, lengths, abs.(Xbns .- d_2), color = teal, label = "2 - asinh-based")
plot!(
    fig, lengths, abs.(Xbns .- Xns);
    color = :gray, linestyle = :dash, label = "the reference in Float64",
)
```

```{julia}
abs.(Xbns .- d_1)
```

```{julia}
abs.(Xbns .- d_2)
```

Below a length of `1` the `asinh`-based version two is the more accurate one: version one returns
`0` for every length up to `1.0e-8`, and at `0.1` its error `9.5e-16` is about a hundred times that
of version two. At `1` the two are equally accurate. From `10` on the order reverses: version one is
off by `8.9e-16` and version two by `4.9e-14`. At `100` the coordinates of `q` are near `1.0e43`,
and the Minkowski metric of `q - p` would need forty-three of their digits where double precision
keeps sixteen, so it comes out as `-2.8e70`, the `max` clamps it to zero and version two returns
`0` instead of `100`, while version one is off by `8.9e-15`. From `1000` on the coordinates of `q`
overflow double precision and both versions return `NaN`. All lengths are measured from
`p = [0, 0, 1]`, where version one reads only the last coordinate of `q`.

## Where to switch between the two versions

To find where version one becomes the more accurate one, we look at distances `s` between `0.01`
and `20`, measured from base points at several distances `r` from `[0, 0, 1]`.
For each pair we draw random directions, compute the points in `BigFloat`, round them to `Float64`,
and average the relative error of both versions to the exact distance `s`.
We plot the errors against `m`, the Minkowski norm of `q - p` that version two computes;
it is related to the distance by ``m = 2\sinh(s/2)``.

```{julia}
#| output: false
function mean_relative_errors(r, s; n = 200, rng = MersenneTwister(42))
    e_1, e_2 = 0.0, 0.0
    for _ in 1:n
        Y = BigFloat.([normalize(randn(rng, 2)); 0])
        pb_r = exp(M, pb, r * Y)
        Z = project(M, pb_r, BigFloat.([randn(rng, 2); 0]))
        qb_s = exp(M, pb_r, s * Z / norm(M, pb_r, Z))
        p_r, q_s = Float64.(pb_r), Float64.(qb_s)
        e_1 += abs(distance_1(p_r, q_s) - s) / s
        e_2 += abs(distance_2(p_r, q_s) - s) / s
    end
    return e_1 / n, e_2 / n
end
radii = [0.0, 1.0, 5.0]
ss = 10.0 .^ range(-2, log10(20); length = 40)
ms = 2 .* sinh.(ss ./ 2)
errors = Dict(r => [mean_relative_errors(r, s) for s in ss] for r in radii)
```

```{julia}
fig2 = plot(;
    legend = :topleft,
    xlabel = raw"$m = 2\sinh(s/2)$ (log. scale)",
    ylabel = raw"mean relative error (log. scale)",
    yaxis = :log,
    xaxis = :log,
)
for (r, ls) in zip(radii, [:solid, :dash, :dot])
    plot!(fig2, ms, max.(first.(errors[r]), 1.0e-20); color = indigo, linestyle = ls, label = "1 - acosh, r = $r")
    plot!(fig2, ms, max.(last.(errors[r]), 1.0e-20); color = teal, linestyle = ls, label = "2 - asinh, r = $r")
end
vline!(fig2, [1.0]; color = :gray, label = raw"$m = 1$")
fig2
```

For all base points the curves cross at about `m = 1`, which corresponds to a distance of
``2\operatorname{asinh}(1/2) ≈ 0.96`` and to ``-⟨p,q⟩_{\mathrm{M}} = 1 + m^2/2 = 1.5``.
Below that the `asinh`-based version two is up to a few hundred times more accurate,
above it the `acosh`-based version one is, and its advantage grows quickly with the distance.

We hence combine both. The switch tests ``-⟨p,q⟩_{\mathrm{M}} > 1.5`` instead of ``m > 1``:
for far apart points the Minkowski metric of `q - p` suffers from the cancellation described above
(at length `100` it is `-2.8e70`), so a test on ``m`` would pick the wrong version exactly where
version two fails.

```{julia}
#| output: false
function distance_3(p, q)
    c = -minkowski_metric(p, q)
    c > 3 // 2 && return acosh(c)
    w = q - p
    return 2 * asinh(sqrt(max(0.0, minkowski_metric(w, w))) / 2)
end
```

which is what `distance` on the
[Hyperbolic](https://juliamanifolds.github.io/Manifolds.jl/stable/manifolds/hyperbolic/)
manifold uses.
On the reference data from above it is as accurate as the better of the two versions
for all lengths up to `100`; for `1000` and `10000` all versions return `NaN`, since `q` overflows.

```{julia}
d_3 = [distance_3(p, q) for q in qs]
finite = isfinite.(d_3)
all(abs.(Xbns .- d_3)[finite] .<= min.(abs.(Xbns .- d_1), abs.(Xbns .- d_2))[finite])
```
